prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the development of long-acting GLP-1-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B042 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The case is that GLP-1 is one of the few complete arcs in modern medicine: the incretin concept, proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1 in humans (Holst), the receptor biology, intestinotropic actions and pharmacology (Drucker), and the engineering of long-acting analogues that made a short-lived gut hormone into a drug (Knudsen). The mechanism is well characterised, the therapeutic effect on glycaemia and weight is large and independently confirmed, and cardiovascular and renal outcome trials now show benefit beyond glucose. Three decades of replication make this mature, and recognition is timely. A prize is most defensible when the physiology and the medicine it produced are both honoured, and here a three-person prize can honour both.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The credited list has four names for a three-person cap, and the literature around GLP-1 peptide identification (Mojsov, and also Habener, who is not credited here) is contested. Excluding Mojsov risks being seen as historically unfair, while excluding Knudsen risks being seen as treating a drug-development contribution as outside the prize. There is also the risk that a prize centred on a commercial product is judged to reward development more than discovery. I do not have verified priority details and rely on recalled literature.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov because Knudsen is a major drug-development figure and the scientific discovery credit is better held by the three, while his second-ranked B006 (TOR, Hall and Schreiber) is placed ahead of CAR-T and optogenetics.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-development point seriously and it is the strongest challenge to my own opening trio. I still keep Knudsen, because here the step from native GLP-1 (minutes of half-life) to a once-weekly drug is itself a scientific achievement in protein chemistry and pharmacology, not routine optimisation, and it is what produced the outcome data that make this prize pressing. I do not think Mojsov's claim is weak, and if the committee's view of the peptide-identification record turns out to be firmer than I can verify, I would accept swapping her in for Knudsen. On B006 I disagree with ranking it second: the biology is foundational, but the clinical consequence is modest next to the leading candidates, and the credit among Hall, Schreiber and Sabatini is less settled than for UPR.

responses.point: Perlmann favours Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for B042, describes Knudsen as drug development rather than discovery, and ranks optogenetics second with a focus on channelrhodopsin discovery plus Deisseroth as the principal neuroscience translator.
responses.response: I agree with the three-person logic on the two scientific anchors, Holst and Drucker, and with his caution that Mojsov's credit is debated in public accounts, which is a reason not to treat her as uncontroversial either. On optogenetics, we both rank it second, but I would not claim that it is close to prize-ready: the six-name credit cannot be fit into three without excluding people with credible claims, and Deisseroth, Boyden and Miesenboeck do not map onto the channelrhodopsin discovery in the same way Nagel and Hegemann do. Because I work on motor circuits, I know how much it changed circuit dissection, but that is exactly why I want to apply the same attribution standard as for any other candidate rather than let familiarity lift it.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, ranks CAR-T second and deep brain stimulation sixth, and sees clinical impact of DBS directly in movement-disorder practice, while noting that single-laureate credit for Benabid omits circuit physiology.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution problem he raises for B012, and I ranked it fifth for that reason: Benabid's observation is decisive, but the subthalamic and basal ganglia circuit knowledge from DeLong and others is not credited, so a one-person prize would misrepresent how this therapy arose. I also disagree with placing CAR-T above UPR, given diffuse attribution (Eshhar is absent from the credited names) and limited efficacy beyond B-cell malignancies; I rank it below B033 for those reasons, though I accept it is the strongest translational alternative to B042 and could be a distinct second part if the committee wants a two-achievement prize.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks UPR second and proposes a two-person CAR-T (June and Sadelain), arguing a two-person prize is cleanest, and ranks nusinersen eighth.
responses.response: I agree with him that Walter and Mori are a clean, compact pair and that UPR is the best-attributed basic-science candidate on the shortlist, which is why it is my first alternative. I am less persuaded that dropping Rosenberg solves the CAR-T attribution problem, since removing a name shortens the list without answering the Eshhar omission. On B027 I am more positive than he is: the Krainer and Bennett pairing is coherent and mechanism-driven, though I recognise the SMN gene discovery sits outside the credit.

uncertainties: Whether the third slot for B042 should be Knudsen or Mojsov, and how to weigh the contested peptide-identification history (Mojsov, Habener) against the drug-development step.
Whether the committee wants a second distinct part with B042, since the three-person cap would then force Knudsen or Mojsov out.
Optogenetics attribution: no three-person subset of the six credited names is free of serious exclusions.
I rely on recalled literature for priority details that I have not verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates from my profile. I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann and a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, but neither is a nominee, and none of the shortlisted candidates is documented as a collaborator, mentee or institutional colleague of mine. Optogenetics is close to my field, but that is topical familiarity and not a personal tie.
